analysis.one_liner: Suspends faster meat and poultry processing line speeds during the COVID-19 emergency.
analysis.headline: The bill, which had 31 cosponsors, never received a vote in any House committee or on the House floor before the term ended in January 2023.
analysis.plain_summary: During the COVID-19 emergency, the bill would have forced meat and poultry plants to slow down. It would have suspended federal waivers that let plants run slaughter lines faster than standard speeds, halted the new swine inspection system that allows those faster speeds, barred the Agriculture Department from approving any further speed increases, and required a government watchdog review of how well workers, food, and animals were protected during the pandemic. It never came up for a vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Meat and poultry plant workers, who process carcasses at high speed in close quarters and faced elevated COVID-19 infection rates during the pandemic; federal meat inspectors, whose staffing and safety the bill protects; consumers of meat, whose food safety depends on thorough inspection; and animal welfare, since faster lines make humane handling harder to verify.

how_it_helps.text: The bill directs the Secretary of Agriculture to suspend all existing waivers allowing faster line speeds at meat and poultry plants and to issue no new ones for the duration of the COVID-19 emergency.
It also suspends implementation of, and conversion to, the New Swine Slaughter Inspection System, the 2019 USDA rule that permitted faster swine slaughter line speeds.
It prohibits the use of any USDA funds during the emergency period to develop or implement any policy that would increase line speeds at covered plants.

After the emergency ends, it requires the Government Accountability Office to review how effectively USDA, Labor, and HHS protected worker, food, and animal safety during the pandemic, including the impact of faster line speeds on worker protections.

It requires the Secretaries of Agriculture, Labor, and HHS to report to Congress by the end of 2021 on pandemic-era actions at covered plants, including spacing, protective equipment, and humane handling enforcement.

analysis.who_pays: Meat and poultry processing companies, which would have to slow slaughter lines, reducing their throughput and per-animal processing revenue for the duration of the emergency, and arguably consumers to the extent slower lines modestly raise processing costs.

drawbacks.text: Slower line speeds mean lower plant throughput during the emergency, which the industry argues raises processing costs and could modestly raise meat prices for consumers.

The bill is a temporary emergency measure: its limits expire when the COVID-19 emergency period ends, after which existing line-speed authority returns, so it does not permanently settle the faster-speeds policy.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is targeted and direct: fewer worker injuries and lower infection risk on high-speed slaughter lines, plus more thorough inspection, during a pandemic that hit meatpacking plants especially hard. The cost is reduced plant efficiency for the duration of the emergency, which may nudge meat prices upward slightly. On balance the tradeoff favors the workers, though the bill's temporary nature means the underlying line-speed policy fight would resume afterward.

outcome.mechanism: The bill sat in committee from the day it was introduced: it was referred to three House committees and two subcommittees, none of which took any further action, and it never reached the House floor before the term ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Rosa DeLauro introduced the bill on March 11, 2021, and it was referred the same day to the Agriculture, Education and Labor, and Energy and Commerce Committees.
On March 12, 2021, it was referred to the Energy and Commerce Subcommittee on Health, and on May 13, 2021, to the Agriculture Subcommittee on Livestock and Foreign Agriculture.
No further action — no hearing, markup, or floor vote — was recorded after those referrals, and the 117th Congress ended January 3, 2023.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Meat and poultry processing companies are better off: the faster line speeds and the new swine inspection system stayed in effect for the entire pandemic period, and no GAO review of worker safety at those speeds was compelled by law.

for.name: Rosa DeLauro
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to suspend increased line speeds at meat and poultry plants during the COVID-19 emergency.

for.name: Jeff Van Drew
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, the only Republican support.

against.name: House Agriculture Committee leadership
against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill after referring it to the Subcommittee on Livestock and Foreign Agriculture; no hearing or markup was ever held.

against.name: House Energy and Commerce and Education and Labor Committee leadership
against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill beyond subcommittee referrals; neither committee considered it.

against.name: Meat and poultry processing industry
against.role: Major processors benefiting from faster line speeds
against.what_they_did: Opposed restrictions on faster slaughter line speeds, which raise plant throughput and revenue.

sides.party_line_note: All 31 cosponsors were Democrats except one Republican; no Republican chairman or committee brought the bill forward, and no roll-call was ever taken.

industries.note: The bill would have suspended the line-speed waivers and the faster swine slaughter system that increase plant throughput, cutting processor revenue during the emergency. Faster lines are also associated with more worker injuries and weaker inspection oversight, so the industry's interest ran against the workers and consumers the bill aimed to protect.
The bill suspends waivers related to inspection staffing requirements, protecting inspector staffing levels and safety during the pandemic.
